key_terms.meaning: The temperature of moist air read by an ordinary dry thermometer; one of the two numbers that fix the state of the air.
Mass of water vapour carried by unit mass of dry air: Y = 0.622 p_w/(P − p_w), where p_w is the water-vapour partial pressure, P the total pressure, and Y is in kg water per kg dry air.
Partial pressure of vapour divided by the saturation vapour pressure at the same dry-bulb temperature: R_H = 100 p_w/p_s, expressed as a percentage.
The temperature to which moist air must be cooled at constant pressure and constant Y before it just becomes saturated; below it, liquid water condenses.
Heat needed to raise 1 kg of dry air plus the vapour it carries by 1 K: c_s ≈ 1.005 + 1.88 Y, in kJ per (kg dry air · K).
Volume occupied by 1 kg of dry air plus its vapour: v_H = (1/29 + Y/18) × 0.08314 T, in m³ per kg dry air, with T in kelvin and 0.08314 in bar·m³/(kmol·K).
Enthalpy of 1 kg dry air plus its vapour referred to 0 °C: H ≈ c_s (t − 0) + 2500 Y, in kJ per kg dry air, where 2500 kJ/kg is the latent heat of vaporisation at 0 °C.
A graph of Y against dry-bulb temperature carrying constant relative humidity, dew-point, wet-bulb and enthalpy lines, so that two known properties fix the state.
The steady temperature reached by air that is contacted with water in an insulated saturator until it leaves saturated, the water being recirculated and its temperature taken as constant.
The temperature shown by a thermometer whose bulb is wrapped in a wet wick and exposed to an air stream; for air–water it equals the adiabatic saturation temperature.

For air–water, h_c/(k_Y c_s) ≈ 1, where h_c is the heat-transfer coefficient in W/(m²·K) and k_Y the mass-transfer coefficient in kg/(m²·s·ΔY); this is why wet-bulb and adiabatic saturation temperatures coincide.
A chamber in which water is sprayed into the air stream, used to humidify, dehumidify, cool or clean the air depending on the water temperature.
A device in which warm water falls through rising air and is cooled mainly by evaporation of a small part of the water, with the rest cooled by the resulting loss of sensible heat.
Range = hot-water temperature − cold-water temperature; approach = cold-water temperature − inlet-air wet-bulb temperature, both in °C.

The dimensionless size number of a cooling tower: KaV/L = ∫ dT_w/(h* − h) taken from cold-water to hot-water temperature, where h* is the enthalpy of saturated air at the water temperature and h the enthalpy of the bulk air, both in kJ per kg dry air.
The moisture content of a solid in equilibrium with air of a given humidity and temperature, in kg water per kg dry solid; the solid neither gains nor loses water at this point.
The average moisture content at which the constant-rate drying period ends and the falling-rate period begins, in kg water per kg dry solid.
Drying in which the hot air is forced through a bed of granular solid rather than across its surface, so the air picks up moisture and cools as it climbs the bed.
A slightly inclined rotating cylinder in which wet solid tumbles along the axis while hot air flows through it, used for free-flowing granular solids in continuous operation.

takeaways: Two numbers, the dry-bulb temperature and the humidity ratio, fix every other property of moist air; the rest are computed, not measured.
The psychrometric chart is only those computations drawn once, so a state is located by any two independent properties and everything else is read off.
For air and water the wet-bulb temperature and the adiabatic saturation temperature are the same because the Lewis relation holds.
Humidifying air with recirculated water follows a constant wet-bulb line, so the adiabatic saturation temperature is the lowest temperature that water alone can reach.
Cooling-tower design integrates an enthalpy driving force between the cold-water and hot-water temperatures, and the answer is the tower characteristic.
A solid stops drying at the equilibrium moisture content of the surrounding air, so that water cannot be removed by that air at any longer time.
Drying time is the area under the curve of 1/(drying rate) plotted against moisture content, taken between the starting and ending moistures.
A dryer design is three balances in a row: water, dry air and heat; sizing of the shell follows from the air velocity the solid can tolerate.
bank_note: Long answers in this unit are mostly chart-and-balance numericals — cooling-tower L/G and characteristic, drying-rate curves, rotary-dryer water and heat balances — plus one descriptive comparison of tower or dryer types, so prepare one worked sum and one comparison for each half.

bank.q: Define absolute humidity, relative humidity, percentage humidity and dew point. Give the unit of each and state how relative humidity and absolute humidity are related.
outline: Absolute humidity Y = 0.622 p_w/(P − p_w), in kg water per kg dry air
Relative humidity = 100 p_w/p_s, a percentage of saturation at the same dry-bulb temperature
Percentage humidity = 100 Y/Y_s, and note it is not the same as relative humidity
Dew point: cool at constant pressure and constant Y until saturated; unit °C
Humidity rises with temperature at constant relative humidity, so the two are not proportional

bank.q: What quantities does a psychrometric chart plot on its axes, and which lines are drawn on it? Explain how two known properties locate the state of moist air and how a third property is then read.
outline: Axes: dry-bulb temperature on the x-axis, humidity ratio Y on the y-axis
Families of lines: constant relative humidity, constant dew point, constant wet-bulb/adiabatic saturation, constant humid volume, and the saturation curve
Any two independent properties, for example dry-bulb and wet-bulb, give one intersection point
At that point, read the humidity, dew point, humid heat and enthalpy directly
Warn that the chart is drawn for one total pressure, usually 1 atm, so it is wrong at other pressures

bank.q: Explain the adiabatic saturation process and show that for the air–water system the wet-bulb temperature equals the adiabatic saturation temperature. State the assumption used.
outline: Insulated saturator, recirculated water, air leaves saturated at t_as
Heat lost by the air equals latent heat of the water evaporated: energy balance written with humid heat and latent heat
Mass balance gives Y_s at t_as in terms of the entering Y and temperatures
Wet-bulb thermometer: convection supplies sensible heat, evaporation takes it away, steady state
Use the Lewis relation h_c/(k_Y c_s) ≈ 1 to show the two temperature equations are identical
Assumption: Lewis relation holds, radiation and conduction along the stem are negligible

bank.q: Distinguish bound, unbound, free and equilibrium moisture in a wet solid. Explain why free moisture is easy to remove but bound moisture may not be removable at all by the given air.
outline: Bound moisture held inside the solid structure by solution or capillary binding, with a lower vapour pressure
Unbound moisture held in the pores, with vapour pressure equal to that of pure water
Equilibrium moisture X* fixed by the temperature and humidity of the air
Free moisture = X − X*, the part that can be removed by that air
Bound moisture needs a lower humidity or a higher temperature before it moves

bank.q: Moist air at 40 °C dry-bulb and 25 °C wet-bulb enters a dryer. Using the psychrometric relations and chart, find the humidity ratio, dew point, relative humidity, humid heat, humid volume and enthalpy of the air.
outline: Use the wet-bulb equation to get Y from t and t_wb
Read or compute Y_s at 25 °C for the saturation term
Dew point from Y by inverting the humidity equation, or from the chart
Humid heat c_s = 1.005 + 1.88 Y
Humid volume v_H = (1/29 + Y/18) × 0.08314 T, T in kelvin
Enthalpy H = c_s (t) + 2500 Y, answer in kJ per kg dry air
State units at every step and note the pressure assumed, usually 1 atm

bank.q: A counter-current induced-draft cooling tower cools water from 45 °C to 30 °C. Air enters at 30 °C dry-bulb and 24 °C wet-bulb and leaves at 38 °C and 90 % relative humidity. Calculate the water-to-air ratio, the number of transfer units and the tower characteristic.
outline: Water balance: L(T_1 − T_2) and the evaporation loss from the humidity rise
Air-side enthalpy in and out from the chart, both in kJ per kg dry air
L/G from the overall enthalpy balance
Integrate KaV/L = ∫ dT_w/(h* − h) step by step in 3–5 °C intervals, h* from the saturation curve at the water temperature
Tabulate 1/(h* − h) against T_w and use the trapezoidal rule
State range = 15 °C and approach = 30 − 24 = 6 °C
Comment on the accuracy of the approximation that L is constant, since some water evaporates

bank.q: A wet solid is dried from 0.35 to 0.05 kg water per kg dry solid in air whose equilibrium moisture content is 0.02. The critical moisture content is 0.15 and the constant drying rate is 2.5 kg/(m²·h) for 1 kg dry solid of 0.6 m² surface. The falling-rate curve is a straight line through the origin. Estimate the total drying time.
outline: Constant-rate period: from 0.35 to 0.15, time = (X_1 − X_c)/(rate per unit area × area per kg)
Identify the falling-rate period from 0.15 down to 0.05, with free moisture X − X*
Linear falling rate in (X − X*): time = (X_c − X*) × ln[(X_c − X*)/(X_2 − X*)] ÷ constant rate
Add the two times and give the answer in hours
Check units: kg water/(kg dry solid) divided by kg water/(h·kg dry solid)

bank.q: A rotary dryer handles 2 tonnes per hour of wet solid, reducing moisture from 30 % to 5 % on a wet basis. Air enters at 100 °C and leaves at 60 °C. Find the water evaporated, the dry-air rate, the heat duty, and estimate the shell diameter and length for an air mass velocity of 2 kg/(m²·s).
outline: Convert wet-basis to dry-basis moisture: X = kg water/kg dry solid, before and after
Dry solid rate is unchanged; water evaporated = dry solid × (X_1 − X_2)
Humidity of entering and leaving air from a heat and mass balance on the dryer
Dry-air rate from the water balance G(Y_2 − Y_1) = water evaporated
Heat duty from the enthalpy rise of the air plus the solid and the water vapour
Diameter from cross-sectional area = air mass rate/(mass velocity), with air density at the mean temperature
Length from a residence time or a volumetric heat-transfer coefficient; state the rule used

bank.q: Air at 35 °C dry-bulb and 20 % relative humidity is blown through an air washer that recirculates its own spray water. Describe the path of the air on the psychrometric chart, find the lowest temperature the water can reach, and estimate the exit condition if the washer is 80 % effective.
outline: Recirculated water takes up the adiabatic saturation temperature, so the air moves along the constant wet-bulb line
Read the entering wet-bulb temperature from the chart, about 19–20 °C for this state
The lowest water temperature is the adiabatic saturation temperature; the air can approach it but not pass it
Effectiveness = (t_in − t_out)/(t_in − t_as), solve for t_out
Humidity rises as the air cools, and it stays below saturation
Explain that a chilled-water spray would move the air below the wet-bulb line and dehumidify it, which is a different operation

bank.q: Compare natural-draft, forced-draft and induced-draft cooling towers, and counterflow with crossflow layouts, in terms of air flow, land area, upkeep and effectiveness. Recommend a type for a large coastal power plant and justify the choice.
outline: Natural draft: tall hyperbolic shell, no fan, low running cost, high capital cost, poor control at part load
Forced draft: fan at the air inlet, higher power, recirculation risk; induced draft: fan at the warm air exit, more stable and easier to control
Counterflow gives better thermal performance per unit volume; crossflow is easier to build and has lower pressure drop
Compare approach, pumping head, drift and makeup water
Recommendation with reasons: induced-draft counterflow, or natural draft where land and capital allow
Mention plume and drift as environmental points

bank.q: A heat-sensitive granular solid must be dried from a high moisture content to a low one. Compare tray, tunnel, rotary and fluidized-bed dryers on contact time, uniformity, dust, and suitability for heat-sensitive solids, and choose one with justification.
outline: Tray: batch, long residence time, low dust, labour heavy, poor for large tonnage
Tunnel: continuous version of tray, first-in first-out, still long times
Rotary: continuous, high throughput, tumbling causes attrition and dust, hold-up is large
Fluidized bed: excellent heat transfer and uniform temperature, short residence time, good for heat-sensitive solids, needs narrow particle size
Choose fluidized bed for heat sensitivity with uniform granules; choose rotary for large tonnage and forgiving solids
Add a note on the falling-rate period being the controlling step

bank.q: Examine the assumptions behind the Lewis relation and hence the wet-bulb thermometer. Under what conditions does the wet-bulb reading become unreliable, and what corrections or precautions are used?
outline: Lewis relation h_c/(k_Y c_s) ≈ 1 holds closely for air–water but not for other gas–vapour pairs
Assumes negligible radiation, negligible conduction along the stem, and air velocity in the working range
High air velocity or hot surroundings add radiation error; shield or use an aspirated psychrometer
Air near saturation gives a small wet-bulb depression, so the humidity derived is inaccurate
Water must wet the wick fully and be free of dissolved solids
Above 100 °C or with superheated vapour, the wet-bulb concept changes and the adiabatic saturation equation is used directly

bank.q: Explain what happens inside a deep bed during through-circulation drying: how the air temperature and humidity change as the air climbs, how the drying zone travels, and what this does to the total drying time compared with cross-circulation.
outline: Air enters hot and dry, picks up moisture in the bottom layer, leaves cooler and wetter
The bed splits into a dried zone, a drying zone and a still-wet zone
As drying proceeds the drying zone moves upward like a front, and the exit air stays near saturation for most of the run
Material near the air inlet reaches equilibrium moisture long before the top layer
Total time is set by the last layer to dry, not by the average rate
Through circulation gives better transfer coefficients and shorter times than cross-circulation, at the cost of higher pressure drop

glossary.def: The general term for the water vapour present in a gas, measured in several ways such as absolute humidity or relative humidity.
The humidity ratio of air that is saturated with water vapour at the given dry-bulb temperature.
One hundred times the ratio of the actual humidity ratio to the saturation humidity ratio at the same dry-bulb temperature.
One hundred times the ratio of the actual water-vapour partial pressure to the saturation vapour pressure at the same temperature.
Moles of water vapour per mole of vapour-free gas, which equals p_w/(P − p_w).
Any operation that increases the water-vapour content of a gas stream.
Any operation that removes water vapour from a gas stream, by cooling below the dew point, absorption or adsorption.
A dehumidification method in which the gas is cooled so that water condenses out, leaving a saturated gas at the lower temperature.
Dehumidification in which the gas contacts a hygroscopic liquid such as lithium chloride solution or glycol, which takes up water.
Dehumidification in which water vapour is held on the surface of a solid such as silica gel or activated alumina.
A humidification method in which live steam is sparged into the air; both the humidity and the temperature rise.
A device in which air passes over a large wetted surface, picking up water vapour without any spray or liquid droplets.
Humidification by compressing the gas and then cooling it, so that a controlled amount of vapour is retained.
Water added to a cooling tower or washer to replace evaporation, drift and blowdown losses.
Fine water droplets carried out of a cooling tower by the air stream, removed by drift eliminators.
The deliberate purging of circulating water to keep dissolved solids below a limit that would cause scaling.
The difference between the dry-bulb and wet-bulb temperatures; it measures how much the air can still take up by evaporation.
The removal of a volatile liquid, usually water, from a wet solid by evaporation into a gas stream.
Water held in the larger pores of a solid whose vapour pressure equals that of free water at the same temperature.
Water held inside the solid by chemical or cellular binding, whose vapour pressure is lower than that of free water.
A plot of the drying rate, in kg water per (m²·h), against the moisture content, showing the warming-up, constant-rate and falling-rate periods.
The drying stage in which the solid surface stays wet and the drying rate stays fixed by the external heat and mass transfer.
The drying stage in which the surface is no longer fully wet and the drying rate drops, controlled by the movement of moisture inside the solid.
A continuous dryer in which trucks or trays of solid move through a long chamber against a stream of hot air.
A dryer in which hot air suspends the particles of solid, giving fast, uniform drying at a nearly constant temperature.
The statement that the heat supplied by the air equals the heat used to evaporate water plus the sensible heat of the solid and the losses.
